# Adhesion and attachment — function ontology

**Card 14 · source workbook `ontology/xlsx/Nature_Adhesion_Ontology_v1.xlsx` · generated by `scripts/build-knowledge.js` — do not edit by hand.**

## Scope boundary

How organisms attach, hold, release and re-attach — wet and dry, reversible and permanent, across scales from molecular to whole-organism. Use for bonding, gripping, sealing against a surface, controlled release and anti-fouling. Adhesion used to close damage belongs to card 10; adhesion as the function itself belongs here. Version 1 — narrower than repair and patterns, and the card says so rather than implying coverage it does not have.

## Strategies

| ID | Strategy | Biological model | Engineering-neutral rule | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NA01 | Split contact into many small contacts | Gecko setae/spatulae; spider scopulae; beetle adhesive hairs | Replace a single large contact with many subcritical contacts so local conformity increases and failure is distributed. | Microfeatures can foul, collapse, or lose contact on very rough surfaces |
| NA02 | Build hierarchy across scales | Gecko lamellae→setae→spatulae; spider branched setae | Allocate different length scales to different jobs: large scales for placement/load transfer, small scales for intimate contact. | Complex fabrication and scale-up; hierarchical defects can dominate failure |
| NA03 | Make adhesion directional / anisotropic | Gecko angled setae and toe curling; spider anisotropic setae | Encode different attachment and release pathways into geometry and loading direction. | Works poorly if load direction is unpredictable or pad cannot orient |
| NA04 | Control system compliance and load path | Gecko soft toe pad + stiff tendon/bone load path; tree-frog… | Design the entire load path, not just the surface: be compliant where contact is needed and stiff where force must be transmitted. | Too much compliance causes creep; too little reduces contact |
| NA05 | Trap and arrest detachment cracks | Fibrillar biological attachment pads; mushroom/film-termina… | Increase adhesion by controlling how failure propagates, not only by increasing bond strength. | Higher toughness can increase release energy |
| NA06 | Use reversible molecular surface anchoring | Mussel foot proteins rich in DOPA/catechol; adhesive peptid… | Use multiple complementary weak/strong interactions at the interface so adhesion survives water and surface chemistry variability. | Oxidation state and curing can trade reversibility for strength |
| NA07 | Combine structural + chemical adhesion | Mussel + gecko hybrids; protein-coated octopus micro-sucker… | Assign contact formation and interfacial bonding to separate mechanisms, then combine them rather than forcing one mechanism to solve both. | More functions increase materials/process complexity |
| NA08 | Phase-separate and deliver adhesive without d… | Mussel adhesive protein coacervates | Separate delivery from curing: first create a dense mobile phase that reaches the target, then lock it in place. | Phase stability window can be narrow |
| NA09 | Dewet the interface before attaching | Leaf beetle underwater attachment using trapped air bubbles | Treat interfacial liquid as an obstacle to remove locally before trying to bond through it. | Gas layer is pressure- and time-sensitive |
| NA10 | Generate wet friction through drainage and ed… | Tree frog / torrent frog toe pads; clingfish discs; octopus… | Manage the interfacial liquid layer rather than ignoring it: provide drainage paths, many edges, compliant contact and/or local pressure di… | Performance depends strongly on fluid properties, roughness and drainage time |
| NA11 | Mechanically interlock after penetration | Porcupine quill barbs; parasite attachment structures | Use asymmetric geometry so entry and removal follow different mechanical pathways. | Invasive attachment can damage substrate |
| NA12 | Change shape after attachment | Spiny-headed worm proboscis; swelling tissue anchors | Decouple placement geometry from holding geometry by transforming only after the interface is established. | Response speed and environmental dependence |
| NA13 | Coordinate multiple adhesive units as a system | Spider opposing legs; gecko multi-digit feet | Optimize the arrangement and coordination of contacts, not only the performance of each contact in isolation. | Requires control/geometry coordination |
| NA14 | Regulate adhesion using environmental conditi… | Bee-collected pollen fluid; spider viscid glue; humidity-re… | Use environmental variables as controllable design inputs, and add a buffering layer when those variables would otherwise destabilize adhes… | Adaptation may be beneficial only within a narrow optimum window |
| NA15 | Switch material state to attach / release | Snail epiphragm; gecko toe motion; octopus active suckers;… | Engineer a large, reliable difference between attachment state and release state rather than compromising at one intermediate adhesion leve… | External trigger, response time and hysteresis add complexity |

## Challenge triggers

| Challenge | Prioritise | Reasoning rule |
|---|---|---|
| C01 Reusable dry attachment on smooth surfaces | NA01 + NA03 | Use split-contact dry adhesion with directional engagement/release. |
| C02 Reusable dry attachment on rough/multiscale surfaces | NA02 + NA04 | Add hierarchy and backing compliance so different scales conform independently. |
| C03 High-load reversible pad at large area | NA04 | Control area-to-compliance ratio and the full load path; use soft contact + stiff load direction. |
| C04 Strong hold but very easy release | NA15 + NA03 | Create distinct attachment and release states using geometry, phase/state change or active actuation. |
| C05 Wet tissue adhesion | NA06 | Use molecular wet anchoring plus tough/compliant backing; separate fast contact from slower curing. |
| C06 Underwater adhesion to smooth surface | NA06 or NA09 | Either bond through water with mussel-like chemistry or locally dewet before contact. |
| C07 Underwater adhesion to rough/curved surface | NA10 + NA04 | Use compliant sealing, distributed suction/friction and geometry that tolerates local gaps. |
| C08 Flooded surface with moving water | NA10 | Drain fluid through channels, increase edge density and maintain compliant wet friction. |
| C09 Interface sees large humidity swings | NA14 | Use environmental response deliberately or add a protective/buffering phase to stabilize water content. |
| C10 Microparticle or fragile-part pick-and-place | NA15 + NA03 | Use switchable geometry/suction with controlled shear/peel release. |
| C11 Temporary tissue fixation with low insertion force | NA11 or NA12 | Use asymmetric barbs or post-insertion shape change so placement and retention mechanics differ. |
| C12 Repositionable high-load industrial assembly | NA15 + NA04 | Use a soft conformal placement state and a stiff/locked holding state that can be reversed on demand. |
| C13 Attachment in vacuum / no liquid allowed | NA01 + NA03 | Favor dry vdW split-contact surfaces and structural compliance control. |
| C14 Dirty/dusty environment | NA01 + NA02 | Use non-tacky split contacts, self-cleaning geometry and controlled detach/reattach cycles. |
| C15 Load direction is uncertain or changes dynamically | NA13 + NA04 | Use multiple independently oriented contacts and coordinate engagement with load vector. |
| C16 Need underwater adhesive delivery into a gap | NA08 + NA06 | Use phase-separated dense adhesive delivery followed by interface anchoring/cure. |
| C17 Need adhesion without residue or surface damage | NA01/NA03 | Prefer dry structural adhesion or state-switching systems with low peel/release energy. |
| C18 Need both adhesion and sensing/active control | NA13 + NA15 | Integrate sensing/actuation so the system verifies seal/contact and adjusts force or release timing. |

## Maturity guide

- **The five levels**
- **Lab-scale** — Demonstrated in a peer-reviewed paper or academic prototype under controlled conditions.
- **Pilot / scaled demo** — Larger device, repeated manufacturing batch, pilot line, field or application-relevant scale; not routine production.
- **In production** — A company or institution manufactures and uses the adhesive technology in a real application. Always state the industry/use case.
- **Commodity** — Multiple suppliers, standard equipment/processes, predictable specifications and cost.
- **N/A — biological mechanism / review** — The row anchors a natural mechanism or synthesis source rather than an engineered implementation.
- **Two mandatory companions**
- **Maturity evidence** — What the level rests on: single paper, multiple groups, patent, pilot, commercial product, or field deployment.
- **Scale-up blocker** — The specific barrier: microfeature yield, contamination, roughness tolerance, coating uniformity, curing time, actuation energy, regulatory approval, tissue damage, or cost.
- **Read this before trusting the column**
- **Citation volume is not maturity** — A seminal or widely cited adhesion paper may still describe only small clean laboratory samples.
- **A patent is not proof of field performance** — Patents show claimed novelty/application intent. They are useful translation evidence but should not be weighted like peer-reviewed performance data.
- **Environment matters** — An adhesive mature on clean glass may be immature on skin, seawater, dusty concrete, vacuum, or rough industrial surfaces.
